core: Who brings a criminal action (a government prosecutor on behalf of the public) versus who brings a civil action (a private party, or sometimes a government suing in a civil posture)
What each action is about: an offense defined by statute against the public order versus a private wrong between parties
The three standards of proof on the American continuum: preponderance of the evidence, clear and convincing evidence, proof beyond a reasonable doubt, and which proceedings use each
Remedies: incarceration, fines, probation and supervision, criminal forfeiture and restitution versus compensatory damages, punitive damages, injunctive and declaratory relief

Constitutional protections that attach in criminal prosecutions and generally not in civil litigation, named but not developed in depth: Fifth Amendment grand jury, double jeopardy and self-incrimination clauses; Sixth Amendment counsel and jury guarantees; the Seventh Amendment civil jury right as the civil-side counterpart
Why one act can produce both a prosecution and a civil suit without violating the Double Jeopardy Clause
The genuinely contested boundary: civil commitment, civil asset forfeiture, punitive damages, and administrative or regulatory penalties
supporting: The Kennedy v. Mendoza-Martinez factors as restated in Hudson v. United States, and the 'clearest proof' threshold for recharacterising a civil sanction as criminal
That an acquittal means the government did not carry its burden, not that a court found the defendant innocent
State-level variation: California Civil Code section 3294 requires clear and convincing evidence of oppression, fraud, or malice before punitive damages may be awarded
Rufo v. Simpson as the standard teaching example of parallel criminal and civil outcomes
outOfScope: Mens rea, actus reus, causation, and the other elements of a crime - owned by criminal-justice-and-criminology:criminal-law-foundations:elements-of-a-crime
Justification and excuse defenses - owned by criminal-justice-and-criminology:criminal-law-foundations:criminal-defenses
Doctrinal depth on the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth Amendments - owned by criminal-justice-and-criminology:criminal-law-foundations:constitutional-protections
Felony, misdemeanor, and infraction classification and grading - owned by criminal-justice-and-criminology:criminal-justice-system:felonies-misdemeanors-and-offenses
Civil procedure mechanics (pleading, discovery, class actions), tort doctrine, and contract doctrine
Non-U.S. legal systems, and the unrelated use of 'civil law' to mean the Roman-derived code tradition

claims.claim: In the U.S. federal system only the government initiates a criminal case, usually through the U.S. attorney's office, while a civil action begins when a party to a dispute files a complaint and serves it on the defendant.

In a criminal trial the burden of proof is on the government and the defendant must be found guilty beyond a reasonable doubt; in a civil case the plaintiff must convince the factfinder by a preponderance of the evidence, meaning that it is more likely than not.

In re Winship, 397 U.S. 358 (1970), explicitly held that the Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime charged; Justice Brennan wrote for the Court, Justice Harlan concurred, and Chief Justice Burger (joined by Justice Stewart) and Justice Black dissented.

Addington v. Texas, 441 U.S. 418 (1979), described three standards of proof across a continuum - preponderance of the evidence for the typical civil case involving a monetary dispute between private parties, an intermediate clear and convincing standard, and proof beyond a reasonable doubt in criminal cases - and held that the Fourteenth Amendment requires at least clear and convincing evidence before a state may involuntarily commit an individual for an indefinite period to a state mental hospital.
Addington identified typical uses of the intermediate standard beyond commitment: civil allegations of fraud or other quasi-criminal wrongdoing, deportation, and denaturalization.

Under 18 U.S.C. 3551(b) an individual found guilty of a federal offense is sentenced to a term of probation, a fine, or a term of imprisonment, and sanctions authorized by sections 3554 (forfeiture), 3555 (notice to victims), and 3556 (restitution) may be imposed in addition; the federal courts describe a sentence as possibly including prison time, a fine paid to the government, and restitution paid to crime victims, with probation officers enforcing conditions of supervision.

In a federal civil case the plaintiff may seek money to compensate for damages, may ask the court to order the defendant to stop the conduct causing the harm, and the court may order other relief such as a declaration of the plaintiff's legal rights.

The Fifth Amendment contains the grand jury requirement for capital or otherwise infamous crimes, the bar on being twice put in jeopardy of life or limb for the same offence, the privilege against being compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against oneself, the Due Process Clause, and the Takings Clause. The Sixth Amendment's guarantees - speedy and public trial, impartial jury, notice, confrontation, compulsory process, and the assistance of counsel - are framed as applying 'in all criminal prosecutions.' The Seventh Amendment preserves the right of trial by jury in suits at common law where the value in controversy exceeds twenty dollars.

Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963), held that the right of an indigent defendant in a criminal trial to the assistance of counsel is a fundamental right essential to a fair trial and is obligatory on the states through the Fourteenth Amendment, overruling Betts v. Brady. Duncan v. Louisiana, 391 U.S. 145 (1968), held that the Fourteenth Amendment guarantees a jury trial in state criminal cases that would fall within the Sixth Amendment's guarantee if tried federally, and that a crime punishable by two years in prison is a serious crime for that purpose.

There is no general right to appointed counsel in civil litigation: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services, 452 U.S. 18 (1981), held that the Constitution does not require appointed counsel for indigent parents in every parental-status termination proceeding, and stated a presumption that an indigent litigant has a right to appointed counsel only when, if he loses, he may be deprived of his physical liberty, with the remaining Mathews v. Eldridge factors balanced against that presumption case by case.

The self-incrimination privilege operates differently across the divide: Griffin v. California, 380 U.S. 609 (1965), held that prosecutorial or judicial comment on a criminal defendant's failure to testify violates the Self-Incrimination Clause as applied to the states, while Baxter v. Palmigiano, 425 U.S. 308 (1976), stated the prevailing rule that the Fifth Amendment does not forbid adverse inferences against parties to civil actions who refuse to testify in response to probative evidence offered against them.

The Double Jeopardy Clause protects only against the imposition of multiple criminal punishments for the same offense, so a criminal prosecution followed by a civil action arising from the same conduct is not double jeopardy.

In Rufo v. Simpson, 86 Cal. App. 4th 573 (2001), the California Court of Appeal recorded that Simpson had been acquitted of the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman in a prior criminal trial, that a civil jury then found he committed the homicides willfully and wrongfully with oppression and malice, that the wrongful-death plaintiffs were awarded $8.5 million in compensatory damages and the two survival actions $12.5 million each in punitive damages, and that the judgments were affirmed. The opinion also noted that none of the civil plaintiffs had been a party to the prior criminal proceeding, in which the parties were Simpson and the People of the State of California.

Federal civil judicial forfeiture is an in rem action against property that requires no criminal conviction, and 18 U.S.C. 983(c)(1) places the burden on the government to establish by a preponderance of the evidence that the property is subject to forfeiture; a claimant asserting the innocent-owner defense bears a preponderance burden as well.

The Supreme Court has classified civil in rem forfeiture differently depending on which constitutional clause is asked: United States v. Ursery, 518 U.S. 267 (1996), held such forfeitures are neither punishment nor criminal for Double Jeopardy Clause purposes, while Austin v. United States, 509 U.S. 602 (1993), held forfeiture under 21 U.S.C. 881(a)(4) and (a)(7) is monetary punishment subject to the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause.

Kansas v. Hendricks, 521 U.S. 346 (1997), held that commitment under the Kansas Sexually Violent Predator Act is civil rather than criminal and therefore raises no double jeopardy or ex post facto problem, reasoning that the scheme is neither retributive nor deterrent and lacks a scienter requirement; Justice Thomas wrote for a five-Justice majority and Justice Breyer dissented on this point, joined by Justices Stevens and Souter and in part by Justice Ginsburg.

Hudson v. United States, 522 U.S. 93 (1997), held that OCC monetary penalties and occupational debarment were civil, so a later criminal prosecution for essentially the same conduct was not barred; it set out the analysis as asking first whether the legislature indicated a preference for the civil or criminal label, then whether the statutory scheme is so punitive in purpose or effect as to transform the civil remedy into a criminal penalty, using the Kennedy v. Mendoza-Martinez factors and requiring 'only the clearest proof' to override legislative intent. The Court largely disavowed the method of United States v. Halper, 490 U.S. 435 (1989), and four Justices wrote separately, concurring only in the judgment.

Punitive damages sit uneasily on the civil side: State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co. v. Campbell, 538 U.S. 408 (2003), stated that although punitive awards serve the same purposes as criminal penalties, defendants subjected to them in civil cases have not been accorded the protections applicable in a criminal proceeding, and held a $145 million punitive award against $1 million in compensatory damages excessive under the Due Process Clause.

State law varies in ways that matter to this distinction: California Civil Code section 3294(a) permits punitive damages only where it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant was guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice, and the Court of Appeal in Rufo described the purposes of such damages as punishing the defendant and deterring similar acts.

The Supreme Court has warned that the civil label is not self-executing: In re Winship, following In re Gault, rejected the 'civil label-of-convenience' attached to juvenile proceedings and said that civil labels and good intentions do not themselves obviate the need for criminal due process safeguards.

Federal felony charges are presented to a grand jury of roughly 16 to 23 members, at least twelve of whom must concur to return an indictment; states are not required to charge by grand jury, and a defendant who is indigent may be represented by a government-provided attorney at no or minimal charge.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether civil in rem forfeiture is 'punishment' for constitutional purposes
positions: United States v. Ursery (1996): in rem civil forfeitures are neither punishment nor criminal for Double Jeopardy Clause purposes, so parallel forfeiture and prosecution are permitted.

Austin v. United States (1993): forfeiture under 21 U.S.C. 881(a)(4) and (a)(7) is monetary punishment and is therefore limited by the Excessive Fines Clause, because the Eighth Amendment's text is not expressly limited to criminal cases.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are current holdings and they are not strictly contradictory - the Court answers the punishment question clause by clause rather than once for all purposes. The lesson presents this as evidence that the criminal/civil line is drawn differently depending on which constitutional question is asked, and cites both opinions rather than asserting a single answer.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether sanctions the legislature calls civil should be treated as punishment
positions: Majority position in Hudson v. United States (1997): the legislative label is the starting point and only the clearest proof that a scheme is punitive in purpose or effect will override it; United States v. Halper's proportionality method is largely disavowed.

Separate opinions in Hudson: Justices Stevens, Souter, and Breyer (joined by Justice Ginsburg) concurred only in the judgment, with Justice Souter and Justice Breyer objecting to the majority's treatment of Halper and to the 'clearest proof' formulation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the governing framework (the Hudson/Ward/Mendoza-Martinez approach) as the law, and separately notes that the Court itself abandoned its own eight-year-old method in Halper and that four Justices declined to join Hudson's reasoning. This is presented as an unsettled question, attributed to the Justices who took each position, with no view offered on which is correct.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether civil commitment of sexually violent predators is punishment
positions: Kansas v. Hendricks (1997) majority: the scheme is civil, is neither retributive nor deterrent, lacks a scienter requirement, and so raises no double jeopardy or ex post facto issue.
Justice Breyer, dissenting in relevant part and joined by Justices Stevens and Souter, and by Justice Ginsburg as to Parts II and III, disagreed.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The holding is stated as the law with the division on the Court reported. The lesson makes no normative claim about whether such statutes are good policy.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive legal content at all - it was topic-agnostic boilerplate about 'organizing information' and 'asking better questions' that named the topic but stated nothing about criminal or civil law. Nothing in it could be verified because nothing in it was a factual claim about the subject.

The draft's vocabulary list defined 'Criminal Law Versus Civil Law' circularly as 'a foundational Criminal Justice & Criminology concept covered in this lesson', and otherwise defined generic study-skills words (context, evidence, application) rather than terms of art in this area.

The draft's Eli-10 analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer') carried no explanatory content and supplied no analogy limits, which this subject requires because the criminal/civil boundary is genuinely contested at its edges.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire lesson with researched content built on primary sources: the constitutional text as published by the National Archives, U.S. Reports opinions read from govinfo PDFs, the U.S. Code as published on govinfo, the California Civil Code from the Legislature's own site, and the federal judiciary's and Department of Justice's descriptions of criminal and civil process.
Added the standard-of-proof continuum with the intermediate clear-and-convincing tier, which the draft omitted entirely and which is the single most testable point in this topic.
Added an explicit statement that this is educational material about U.S. law and not legal advice, and an explicit note that state law varies - both required by this subject's review profile.

Added the contested-boundary material (civil commitment, civil forfeiture, punitive damages, administrative penalties) with citations to the specific opinions, rather than presenting the criminal/civil line as clean.

Verified the vote and authorship of every cited opinion against the U.S. Reports text rather than relying on a summary. An automated summary of In re Winship attributed the majority opinion to Justice Blackmun; the opinion itself shows Justice Brennan delivered it, and Blackmun had not yet joined the Court when it was decided. That error was caught and corrected before drafting.

Kept mens rea, defenses, offense classification, and amendment-by-amendment doctrine out of the lesson because later topics own them; the constitutional provisions are named here and their depth is handed off.

sourceRecords.title: In re Winship, 397 U.S. 358 (1970)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office, United States Reports volume 397 (govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Official U.S. Reports text downloaded and read in full. Used for the explicit holding that the Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime charged; for the case posture (a 12-year-old adjudicated delinquent under the New York Family Court Act on a preponderance standard, section 744(b)); for the Court's rejection of the 'civil label-of-convenience' and its statement that civil labels and good intentions do not themselves obviate the need for criminal due process safeguards; for the Court's rejection of the argument that the difference between the standards is 'tenuous'; and for Justice Harlan's concurrence explaining why preponderance suits a civil suit between private parties (society views an erroneous verdict for either side as roughly equally serious) while the criminal standard shifts almost the entire risk of error onto the government. sourceRecords.title: Addington v. Texas, 441 U.S. 418 (1979)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office, United States Reports volume 441 (govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Official U.S. Reports text read in full. The lesson's primary authority for the three-standard continuum: preponderance of the evidence for the typical civil case involving a monetary dispute between private parties, because society has a minimal concern with the outcome and the litigants share the risk of error roughly equally; proof beyond a reasonable doubt in criminal cases, where society imposes almost the entire risk of error upon itself; and an intermediate standard usually combining the words clear, cogent, unequivocal and convincing, typically used in civil cases alleging fraud or other quasi-criminal wrongdoing and in deportation and denaturalization cases. Also used for the holding that a clear and convincing standard is required by the Fourteenth Amendment before indefinite involuntary commitment to a state mental hospital, for the Court's refusal to require beyond a reasonable doubt in that setting, for the observation that states remain free to use a higher standard, and for the Court's candid note that there were no directly relevant empirical studies of how jurors apply the three tests. Burger, C.J., wrote for all participating Members; Powell, J., took no part.

sourceRecords.notes: Read because law.justia.com and courtlistener.com both blocked direct automated retrieval; the Internet Archive capture of 27 December 2023 was used instead, and the record is marked reference only for that reason even though the underlying opinion is a government edict. Used for: the statement that in a prior criminal trial Simpson was acquitted of the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman while in the civil trial the jury concluded he killed them, having acted willfully and wrongfully with oppression and malice; the awards of $8.5 million compensatory damages on the wrongful death cause of action and $12.5 million punitive damages on each of the two survival actions; the disposition affirming the judgments, decided 26 January 2001 with review denied 25 April 2001; the observation that the parties to the prior criminal proceeding were Simpson and the People of the State of California represented by the Los Angeles County District Attorney, and that none of the civil plaintiffs had been a party to it; and the court's restatement that the purposes of punitive damages under California law are to punish the defendant and deter similar acts. No wording from the page is reproduced.
